options: A remote server that stores repository backups
A script Git runs automatically at a specific point in its workflow, such as before a commit
A GitHub feature for linking issues to PRs
A type of merge conflict marker
questions.explain: A Git hook is a script tied to a specific event in Git's workflow (pre-commit, pre-push, etc.) that runs automatically when that event occurs.

questions.q: Why doesn't a pre-commit hook automatically exist on a teammate's machine just because they cloned the same repository?
options: Hooks are stored in a public cloud database shared by all clones
Hooks can only be created by repository administrators
Git automatically disables hooks after the first clone
.git/hooks/ lives inside the .git folder, which Git itself does not track or version — so hook scripts aren't part of the cloned history
questions.explain: The .git/hooks/ folder is not tracked by Git — it's excluded along with the rest of .git's internal state — so each clone starts with Git's unused .sample hooks only, unless a team's tooling installs the real scripts separately.

questions.q: What happens if a pre-commit hook script exits with a non-zero status?
options: Git aborts the commit entirely
Git ignores the exit code and commits anyway
Git automatically fixes the lint errors
Git deletes the staged files
questions.explain: A non-zero exit status from a pre-commit hook tells Git the check failed, which blocks the commit from completing until the issue is resolved (or the hook is bypassed).

questions.q: What does running git commit --no-verify do?
options: Forces all hooks to run twice
Verifies the commit against the remote server before completing
Skips the commit's hooks entirely, including pre-commit
Automatically signs the commit with a GPG key
questions.explain: --no-verify deliberately bypasses a commit's hooks, which is exactly why client-side hooks alone aren't a guarantee — a required CI check on the server is needed as the actual enforced backstop.

questions.q: Why do real teams typically pair client-side hooks with CI-based status checks, rather than relying on hooks alone?
options: Because hooks are slower than CI checks
Because hooks can be skipped or simply never installed on someone's machine, while a required CI check runs on the server regardless
Because GitHub does not support hooks at all
Because CI checks replace the need for a .git folder
questions.explain: Client-side hooks are a local convenience that a developer can bypass or simply never set up; a required CI check on the server runs unavoidably for every PR, making it the actual guarantee a team can rely on.
